climbing_route.label: Snowfield and scree to the ridge crest
climbing_route.notes: From the stance in Horseshoe Basin, gain the snowfield at the base of the peak, then work left across scree and scramble easy blocky ground before dropping into a gully and following it up to the crest of the ridge linking Horseshoe with the Lick of Flame. Two variations of this section are described and both go at 3rd class; the terrain is loose throughout, so parties should stay off one another's fall line and avoid stacking up in the gully. Early in the season the snowfield at the base can be firm enough to want crampons as well as an axe.

climbing_route.label: Narrow summit ramp
climbing_route.notes: From the crest a narrow ramp leads up and climbers' left toward the summit. It begins as exposed 3rd-class ledge travel on scree-covered rock with a long drop below; the ramp is the only reasonable line to the top, and stepping off it puts you on steeper broken ground. Route-finding trap: the historical Horseshoe is the twin-spired formation with the U-shaped notch on Ripsaw Ridge, and neighbouring towers on the same ridge look plausible from below.

climbing_route.label: Summit step
climbing_route.notes: The ramp turns 5th class just under the top — a short steep move gains the roughly metre-square notch that is the summit. Reported as an easy Grade II, 5.2, usually climbed as a single pitch of about 100 ft; a 60 m rope and a light rack of cams protect it, with an anchor built at the base of the step. Aged webbing has been found on the summit and parties commonly make one single-rope rappel back down the ledge before reversing the scramble. This is a long day to carry a rope for a few metres of 5th class, but the exposure at the step is real and the rock is only moderately trustworthy.

climbing_route.label: Saddle traverse to the access notch
climbing_route.notes: From the saddle at roughly 6,800-6,900 ft the line does not go straight up: parties drop about 200 ft down the south side, traverse east to a notch, round the ridge and cross a broad gully. That gully holds notably bad rock and is the first place a dislodged block reaches the party below — softball-sized rock has been knocked down here. Snow lingering in the gullies into midsummer can force the traverse out onto steep south-facing slopes instead.

climbing_route.label: Rib and lower crest steps
climbing_route.notes: Gain a rib near 7,100 ft and follow the crest, or just right of it, on 3rd-class scrambling. Two steps interrupt it: a step of about 30 ft with an overhang on its left and a slanting ramp on the right, climbed at roughly 5.0 via the ramp, and above that a short buttress of about 15 ft at 4th class. The rock here has a pillowy texture that makes nuts, cams and slings largely useless, so this is protectable only in places and much of it is effectively soloed.

climbing_route.label: Narrow summit ridge
climbing_route.notes: From about 7,600 ft the ridge narrows sharply and the exposure becomes severe, with scree-covered ledges where a single slip would be unsurvivable. The north face falls away almost vertically for about 1,000 ft on the left, so the line stays right of the crest throughout; wandering left is the serious route-finding error here. Parties consistently report this section as harder on the descent than the ascent.

climbing_route.label: Summit headwall step and chimney finish
climbing_route.notes: The crux is a short bulging step of roughly 12-15 ft close to the summit, reached from a wide slanting ledge. It is steeper than its 5.6 rating suggests, the rock is crumbly, and natural protection is essentially absent; fixed bolts are in place on the platform and at an overhanging traverse below, and are used for rappelling on the way down. Above the step, class 3-4 ground including a short chimney with good solid holds leads through a class 2-3 gully for the last 100 ft to the top.

climbing_route.label: Bergschrund and gully to the ridge toe
climbing_route.notes: Leave the Terror Glacier at the bergschrund below the west end of the peak and climb roughly 300 ft of gully to reach the toe of the west ridge, where the roped climbing begins. The schrund and the moat where snow meets rock are the variable part: they open through the season and the crossing is easiest with continuous snow early. Total climbing above this point is about 1,300 ft, called Grade III with 14 pitches.

climbing_route.label: Lower ridge corners and lichen ledges
climbing_route.notes: The first pitches work through corner systems and lichen-covered ledges on compact rock. The compactness is the problem — placements are scarce and where one is available it should be taken rather than run past. Loose blocks sit on the ledges through this section and the standard practice is to clear them deliberately once the second is out of the fall line rather than leave them for a following party.

climbing_route.label: Ridge proper
climbing_route.notes: Above the lower corners the line gains the ridge crest itself, where the rock quality improves steadily pitch by pitch and is described as extremely good on the crest. Climbing is sustained at the grade rather than concentrated in one crux, so it is the accumulated length rather than any single move that governs the day; a party's speed here decides whether the descent happens in daylight.

climbing_route.label: Summit headwall
climbing_route.notes: The route finishes up the right-hand side of the headwall on good rock to the summit ridge. A rack of a single set from about 0.1 to 3 inches with doubles from 0.3 to 1 inch, plus extra cord and a few pins, and a single 60 m rope, is what parties carry. Descent is by rappel: stations on the west side of the summit lead back down the west ridge, ending with a rappel of about 100 ft onto the glacier, and multiple parties report six full-length rappels on twin ropes. Retreat from high on the route is therefore possible but slow, and the heavily crevassed Terror Glacier still has to be recrossed afterwards.

climbing_route.label: Bergschrund and rock step
climbing_route.notes: The base is guarded by a bergschrund and, later in the season, a moat where the snow has pulled back from the rock. Parties report a short lead of 4th to easy 5th class rock to clear it, and separately several 4th-class moves in the steep gully above the moat; which of these you get depends entirely on how much snow remains. Snow bridges here are thin and receding by midsummer, and rappel slings have been found on the east side of the constriction. Late in the season the face below loses its snow and turns slabby, which is when the moat becomes the deciding problem.

climbing_route.label: South-facing snow face
climbing_route.notes: Above the schrund, several hundred feet of 40- to 55-degree snow lead to the top of the face. It is a south-facing slope, so it is icy in the pre-dawn shade and softens fast once the sun is on it — parties leave the col around 4 a.m. specifically to be off it before the heat, and more than one has wished for a second tool on the ice. The angle is steep enough that a slip would not be arrested, and the schrund is directly below. Descending is the harder direction; expect to downclimb the steps you kicked and to make at least one rappel over the schrund.

climbing_route.label: Summit ridge
climbing_route.notes: From the top of the face gain the southwest ridge, from which the summit is essentially a walk with easy scrambling. The rock on top is crumbly and the summit is elongated, so the true high point is genuinely hard to pick out — one party found no register and could not confirm which bump was highest. Cairns mark a line back down the ridge toward the col, which some parties use instead of reversing the gully; old rappel anchors there have been found needing backup webbing.

climbing_route.label: Hanging glacier from Luna Cirque
climbing_route.notes: The route is the original line on the peak, taken from Luna Cirque, and the name is informal — it refers to the hanging glacier ringing the cirque rather than an officially named ice body. From the cirque there is a substantial amount of snow climbing: ascend the glacier immediately south of the peak and continue up it where it narrows and steepens as it flows down from higher on the mountain. This hanging glacier is the crux of the whole route and can be impassable in late season, so timing is the main decision the route asks of a party.

climbing_route.label: Rock step to the upper snowfield
climbing_route.notes: Where the narrows end, turn north and climb over a rock step to reach the highest snowfield on the peak. This is the transition from snow to rock and the point at which the party commits to the upper route; the whole climb above the cirque is only about 400 ft in four pitches, so the step is short, but it is what stands between the glacier and the upper mountain.

climbing_route.label: Slabs to the ridge
climbing_route.notes: Two to three pitches of easy slab climbing lead from the upper snowfield to the ridge. Parties carry runners and a few pieces of gear rather than a full rack, which reflects how sparse the placements are on slab — protection is where the features allow rather than where you want it. Helmet and rope are listed as standard for this section.

climbing_route.label: Summit block
climbing_route.notes: A summit block of about 25 ft finishes the route; the climbing overall is rated 4th class with a move of easy 5th, Grade II. Descent is by downclimbing the route back to the snow, with rappels recommended for the steeper sections. Because the hanging glacier below has to be recrossed to get home, a party that finds it in poor condition on the way up should treat that as the turnaround decision rather than pressing on.

climbing_route.label: Broad ridge to the false summit
climbing_route.notes: From Luna Col at about 7,200 ft the route climbs the broad ridge above on roughly 1,100 ft of class 2 to 3 talus and scree to the false, southern summit. The rock is loose in places and parties are advised not to stack up beneath one another. Snow lingers on and just below the false summit well into the season and is often the first unavoidable snow of the ascent, so an axe is worth carrying even when the lower slopes are dry. Poles are commonly left here.

climbing_route.label: Connecting ridge to the true summit
climbing_route.notes: The true summit lies beyond a short connecting ridge that is the only technical part of the peak. Drop roughly 5 ft off the false summit and scramble a narrow, very exposed 4th-class crest: a snow-covered cliff falls several hundred feet down the northwest face on one side and a snow-free cliff drops the southeast face on the other. A commonly used variation avoids the most exposed traverse by dropping onto a ledge on the southeast side, scrambling back to the ridge behind the summit and finishing with a few 4th-class moves from the back. Descent reverses the route; there is no water above the Access Creek basin, so the summit push is done on what you carry.

climbing_route.label: Snow gully to the west ridge
climbing_route.notes: From the Terror Glacier below the spires, climb the steep snow and ice gully that gives access to the west ridge, topping out at the col at roughly 7,200 ft between Inspiration Peak and West McMillan. Axe and crampons are used here even by parties who crossed the glacier unroped. Late in the season the gully loses its snow and the top of it can hold a moat where the snow has pulled back from the rock; earlier it is firm and holds better.

climbing_route.label: Scree and heather ridge
climbing_route.notes: Above the gully the ridge relaxes into a long, mellow 3rd- to 4th-class scramble on scree, heather and more scree. The footing is poor and rockfall onto a party strung out below is the main hazard on this stretch; there is no sustained difficulty, but the loose ground makes it slow both up and down. The overall route is rated 4th class, Grade II, about 2,000 ft.

climbing_route.label: Summit block and final ridge
climbing_route.notes: A short section of exposed 3rd-class climbing leads onto the summit block. It starts loose and scree-covered but the rock improves markedly toward the top; the exposure is concentrated in the last few moves between the false summit and the true summit, where the ridge narrows and drops away steeply into McMillan Cirque on one side and toward Terror Basin on the other. Some parties fix a hand line for that stretch. Descent reverses the route, including downclimbing the snow gully back to the glacier.

climbing_route.label: Bergschrund entry at the base
climbing_route.notes: The face begins near 8,500 ft on the northwest side, bounded by the Roman Nose on the climber's right and serac walls on the left. Getting established means crossing a bergschrund, and there are two on the route; depending on the year the crossing can involve a very short vertical step and is often the most committing and least reversible move of the day. Two general lines exist: the right-hand one has more crevasses and schrunds but far less overhead exposure and is the usual recommendation, while it melts out and becomes unreliable from around the start of July; the left-hand line is threatened by icefall from the seracs for its lower half.

climbing_route.label: Lower face, moderate snow and ice
climbing_route.notes: Most of the lower and middle face runs at 40 to 50 degrees on snow and alpine ice with occasional short steeper steps, and is commonly simul-climbed by competent parties to save time. Depending on the line chosen the middle either follows an ice arete or takes long moderate slopes broken by large crevasses. Protection is pickets in soft snow and screws where ice is exposed, with long runners; signs of avalanche activity have been noted on the face. Being here after sunrise is the main hazard — the upper mountain begins shedding ice and rock as it warms, and even small pieces can knock a climber off, so pre-dawn starts are standard.

climbing_route.label: Upper headwall ice
climbing_route.notes: The upper roughly 800 ft is the sustained part: ice reported at around 60 degrees, rated in the AI3-4 and WI3 range, with short vertical steps. Reliable protection is scarce here — above the second rock band the ice is thin enough over rock that pickets get punched through it rather than set — so this section is usually pitched out with screw belays rather than simul-climbed. Parties should expect to be moving steadily on 45 to 50 degree ice for around a dozen pitches with the steeper steps on top of that, and to carry a pair of technical tools each.

climbing_route.label: Exit to the summit plateau
climbing_route.notes: The angle kicks back near 10,200 ft, but the final ice face is broken by a large bergschrund that can give the steepest and most exciting climbing on the route depending on how it has opened. Above it, easier ground leads onto the summit plateau. Eight to twelve hours from camp to the top is typical. There is no reasonable retreat down the face once established on the upper headwall, and the standard descent is the Coleman-Deming route on the other side of the mountain rather than a reversal, so the plan has to account for getting back around to camp.
